Short answers and practical tips for using 2-Stroke Calc – calculators, vehicles, account and Pro version.
The app offers various calculators for common 2-stroke engine calculations. You can find all available modules in the calculator overview.
Calculator inputs are processed locally and not stored permanently. With an account, vehicle data (master data, maintenance, fuel log) is synced to the cloud.
What units does the app use?
Each calculator uses fixed units suited to the calculation – mostly metric (mm, cc, °, km/h, etc.). There is no option to switch between metric and imperial units.
How do I change the menu layout?
Go to Settings → Appearance → Menu type to switch between bottom menu and side panel.
Some modules are part of the Pro version – by default vehicles, port timing, wire gauge, liquid calculator and gearbox. You can buy them via Google Play or use them with an unlocked account.
Why do I need an account?
An account enables cloud sync for your vehicles, Pro purchase via Google Play and profile management. You can use calculators without an account.
They remind you of due maintenance, MOT dates and expiring insurance for your vehicles. You can change the permission anytime under Settings → Permissions.

Rectangular: high peak power and rpm, strong resonance kick – low durability.
Rectangle with rounded corners: area = W×H − (4−π)×r².
Oval: wider power band, less peak power – high durability with rounded top edge.
Trapezoid: compromise between oval and rectangular – larger blowdown time-area without losing useful stroke.
Triangle – base at top, apex centred at bottom (boosters): area = top width × height / 2.
V-shape – apex at bridge (UT), slanted outer edge (twin exhaust): area = top width × height / 2 per window.

Widest point at top (TDC) – guide: ~65%% cast rings, ~70%% chrome rings, series 125 cc ~89%%
Chord span relative to bore diameter
Total bottom width incl. bridges – 125 cc example: 10 mm per window at BDC
A narrow BDC width keeps the port tract slim; widening at the top has more impact on time-area
Chord ≤ 65%% – conservative, suitable for cast rings.
Chord ~65–70%% – everyday use, e.g. chrome-plated steel rings.
Chord ~70–90%% – series sport (125 cc example: 48 mm / 54 mm ≈ 89%%).
Chord > 90%% – tuner territory (up to ~95%% possible), watch ring stress.

Widening at the top affects time-area much more than at the bottom, because the piston keeps the upper region open longer. This increases blowdown without shortening useful stroke. Widen at the bottom only if you cannot reach enough cross-section otherwise.

Oval: wide band, mild kick. Rectangular: peak power, strong resonance kick, low durability. Trapezoid: usually the best compromise. Trapezoid derivatives (bridge, auxiliary ports): maximum band at high power.
Series 125 cc twin trapezoid: 10 mm per window at BDC, 48 mm chord span (≈ 89%% of bore). Straight top edge for a strong pressure wave, narrow BDC width for a slim port tract.

The wider the exhaust, the higher the ring stress. A curved top edge and angled side walls (trapezoid/oval) are easier on rings. Bridges allow straighter edges but cost flow – you may need slightly more cross-section.
